There were thousands of toys left over from the vast benefits raised for the children of the poor, and yesterday, at the 69th regimen armory, a second Christmas festival was held so that the balance of these toys could be distributed. The big party was held under the auspices of the Bureau of Recreation, Department of Parks. Having found a many good little boys and girls on Christmas Eve, on his trip from house to house, Santa Claus was especially pleased to make farewell presentations, before returning to the cold regions from which he emanates. Over one thousand children participated in the festivities, during which all kinds of toys and od things to eat were given away. The various pork playgrounds, decorated tables for their own sections and competed for a prize given for the most elaborately decorated table. All the children, after leaving the armory, with stomachs filled with Goodies and arms filled with toys, felt indebted to the members of the Good Fellow Club who were chiefly responsible for the good times provided. I was so desperately poor and he so rich! So miserable—an underpaid companion to a cantankerous woman, who hated me because I was not as hideous as she was!"
Martindale hardly recognised her voice with this new metallic note in it.

"It was in Cairo that I learned the truth. We had been married a year," she said. "We were staying at Shepheard's Hotel, and it was Lord Bobby Fristen—you remember Bobby?—who pulled all the fabric of my dreams about me. You see, the Fristens were cousins of the poor dead lad, and Bobby remembered Vivian Carr, who called himself John Saxe... He cut him dead there before everyone—it was very bitter in the eating. that golden-coated, dead-sea fruit that I had grasped so eagerly."

"That was the end and the beginning," she said. "I learned what contempt and hatred were on that hotel verandah. I couldn't forgive him—there are some things that are not forgivable. All his kindness, all his virtues—and he had many—weighed as nothing in the balance. He would have told you I drove him to drink—perhaps I did—I know I seemed to turn to a woman of stone." "My poor Kitty," Martindale said.

"Happy Kitty!" She spoke fiercely. "I am not going to pretend that I am sorry I am free! This old, sordid story—I should never have told it, only now—don't you see his obsession is to be our Salvation?"

He saw—her hope and that was all. At Nobyoro, where Saxe had purchased his vast estates, they would live in primeval solitude; John Saxe would become more and more of a name, and presently even his name would be forgotten.

But in his heart was kindled no hope, and only his love and her nearness kept him from despair. Exile, self-obliteration—they seemed all at once to recede before a new fear that rose up in his heart. A fear that was crystallised in a saying:—"The evil that men do lives after them. . . . " This evil thing that the man he had known as John Saxe had done—was it dead and interred with him? Or would it ever rise again to menace he man who had taken his name? (To be continued.)

STANLEY SHOW FIASCO.
Few Exhibits at the Annual Cycle Display at the Agricultural Hall.

There is war in the cycling camp. For something like thirty-five years the Stanley Show in November has been the Mecca of all good wheelmen—first at the Athenæum; later at the now demolished Aquarium, at Westminster; and, for something over twenty years at the Agricultural Hall.

There have been fights in the past. The manufacturers have wanted to get the show into their own hands, as Mr. T. Lough, M.P., suggested yesterday, for interested motives. The Stanley Club, who look upon themselves as trustees to the public for the funds accumulated at previous shows, will spend their money on behalf of the public.

will spend their money to be buried. The show this year is a failure. Next year the Stanley Club will probably offer to the public one of the best shows ever seen. This winter they have been taken by surprise, too late, and in a way their honorary organisation has broken down.
